studies.title: The Prayer That Opens Everything
studies.meaning: These seven lines are a prayer God teaches, so a person knows how to speak to Him. Praise comes first. Then two names of mercy. Then ownership of the day when accounts are settled. Only halfway through does the speech turn from talking about God to talking to Him. Only then does it ask. The one request is for direction, not for relief or wealth. Early scholars read the rest of the Quran as its answer.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Mecca. It is among the earliest complete surahs given to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). Those were the years when a small, pressured community was learning to pray at all. A few classical reports place a second revelation in Medina. Early scholars note the difference and leave it open. From the first written collections, it stood at the head of the book rather than in order of revelation.

keyTerms.note: The definite article makes it total. It is not an act of praise someone chooses to offer. It is praise as such, all of it, belonging to God whether or not anyone gives it.

It is built on a root shared with the word for womb. It names a mercy that is vast and unearned, there before anything anyone does, spread over everything created. The Quran uses it almost as a second name.
Not a narrow footpath but a wide public road, the kind a caravan travels. The word carries openness and easy passage. So the request is for a road wide enough to walk without stumbling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca lived by the road. Merchants left for Syria in summer and Yemen in winter. A caravan's survival turned on whether the guide knew the route. A wrong turn meant days without water. Asking to be shown a straight road was not first a metaphor. It was the most practical request a traveller could make. This prayer puts it in the mouth of everyone who says it.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only surah spoken entirely from the human side to God, rather than from God to people. That is why early scholars call it a prayer taught, not a message sent. The classical tradition records more than twenty names for it. Among them are the Mother of the Book, the Cure, and the Seven Oft-Repeated named in surah fifteen.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Praise, mercy and judgement come before the request. That sets an order the whole Quran keeps: God is known before He is asked. The voice is plural, so there is no room for a purely private religion. Even someone praying alone speaks as part of a community. The request itself admits that guidance is not something a person makes and keeps. It is asked for daily by people who already have it.

crossReferences.why: Names this surah the seven oft-repeated verses, given along with the whole Quran.
Calls the straight path God's own, and warns about the side roads that scatter travellers.
Ties worship to remembering God, the move this prayer makes from speaking about God to standing before Him.

studies.applyIt: You probably say these lines several times a day, faster than you can think them. Tomorrow, slow down at the sixth line, the request for a straight road. Hold it for one extra breath before moving on. Notice what you were about to ask for instead. The order of this prayer was given before the asking. It is worth arriving at the request unhurried.
studies.explainEasier: These lines are a prayer God taught people to say. First you praise God and call Him kind. Then you ask for one thing: show me the right way to live.
